233.t: Why he resisted the electric bass
233.s: Monk had once seen an electric bass in Indianapolis and thought it the worst thing for music, so he left his upright in its cover.
233.q: He must have thought of that before I showed up, because otherwise he could have told me on the phone, 'Don't bring the upright.'

233.t: How long to get comfortable with the electric bass
233.s: He cannot say when it clicked, only that it took months and a mental adjustment; he had to play with good feeling and time.
233.q: Well, I can't put a time period on it because as I think back, it just happened. Things have a way of happening over a period of time, how... I don't know how to answer that.

233.t: A 'freak instrument': reactions of bandmates and audiences
233.s: He worked for good tone and pitch, bandmates accepted it, and audiences searched the stage for where the bass sound came from.
233.q: Because when I was beginning... Yeah, right, when I began to play. But I was very serious about it. Number one, I had to be in tune, the thing had to... I wanted to be in tune. I didn't want to be critical because of that. I didn't want to be critical because it was too loud, because it was an…

233.t: Hampton turns up the amp and Monk turns it down
233.s: Hampton liked hearing the bass and would turn up the amp; Monk quietly turned down his own control.
233.q: See, because Hamp, when we were traveling with Hamp, Hamp liked that sound because he could hear the bass. Really hear the bass. Now, you had to realize, then, when there was

233.s: With nobody else playing electric bass he had no one to compare notes with, which made him more conscious as a player.
233.q: : And that experience of being in the company of...that type thing was great for me. It also made me be more conscious of the instrument, I think, during that period. Because it was

233.t: Fender promotion and the European tour
233.s: Fender supplied bass and amp; Monk got more newspaper write-ups than Hampton in Europe, but called it Hampton's creation.
233.q: : Yes, I was very close with them because once I started playing the instrument, when I was in California I would always go out, because we kept a close relationship for promotional purposes. They furnished the amplifier and the bass so they would constantly be on top of it. And with a person like…

233.t: Bass players who criticized the electric bass
233.s: Monk says upright players saw it as a threat and that it is a different instrument, not a replacement.
233.q: Mainly bass players, because it was a threat to a bass player. It wouldn't be a threat to another person. And I can understand it. I really...that's the way I felt about it when I first saw it. I was very closed-minded about it. And didn't want to open my mind to accept it because...

233.s: He had not chosen the transition and still longed for the upright bass.
233.q: Yeah, I did. I had some periods where I was threatening to go back to the upright, because I didn't make the move by choice. It wasn't my...It wasn't by choice that transition, you see. And I always felt like the upright bass was still my instrument.

233.t: Three months with Georgie Auld at the Tailspin
233.s: Auld at first was dismayed by the electric bass, then loved it after the first tune, and begged Monk not to leave.
233.ch: Leaving Hampton: Europe and Los Angeles
233.q: I swear to God, when I played that first tune, he turned around and said, 'Yeah!' and went straight ahead from then on. He begged me not to leave the group when I finally left.

233.t: Going back to the upright bass
233.s: Having played electric only for others, Monk bought an upright to find out where he stood, contrasting Wes's guitar.
233.q: : So we had a brand new station wagon and we were ready to go out as the Montgomery Brothers. Now, this is the interesting period because, I'm saying, finally, 'Well, I'm going back to the upright bass.'

233.t: Lugging an amplified upright against the congas
233.s: The upright was drowned out, forcing Monk to carry a big amp and bass.
233.ch: Wes's death and Monk's turning point
233.q: I was still fighting this image of trying to play the upright bass. I wasn't that unhappy with it at this point, but I just couldn't get...Here I am complaining again. Because the sound was so strong. When you think about how firm and heavy Wes played, with the congas...and Buddy was a strong…

233.t: The no-drums trio with electric bass
233.s: Monk feared Red expected an upright but Red wanted the electric bass; the three weeks turned into about a year and a half.
233.q: The three weeks went into two years. It was a little less than two years, about a year and a half, or nine months, something like that. But it was so strange because when I...it didn't dawn on me what we were doing instrumentation-wise. In fact, I wasn't sure he was...I thought he was going to use…

233.t: Chosen because of the shortage of bassists
233.s: Monk says they used him since no real bassist was available, but he played well after the second year.
233.q: consideration, there was such a shortage of bass players. You see what I'm saying. They wouldn't have chose me over Ray Brown, if Ray Brown was there. They wouldn't have chose me over Ron Carter or over someone, but just...they weren't there. That doesn't mean I was bad; my playing was bad, that…

70.t: Franz Jackson's arrangement for two basses
70.s: Franz Jackson wrote a number for two basses and Jackson and Hinton played it together, Hinton on three-quarter bass and Jackson on the big bass.
70.q: Yeah, uh-huh. -- so I asked you, I said, "Milt," I said, "let me try this with you." So Milt looked at me and he said, "All right," you know, and said, you know -- so I went up there and we had a ball.

70.t: John Kirby and the tuba fading out
70.s: Jackson first saw Kirby with Fletcher in 1930 playing both tuba and bass, and he was the first tuba player with lip vibrato.
70.ch: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
70.q: Yes, I knew John Kirby. John Kirby, why, I first saw him with Fletcher's band in 1930 down in Cincinnati, he had his tuba and his bass fiddle. Now, he was the first tuba player I heard play a lip vibrato on the tuba, and it was pretty. It was pretty, although he didn't play tuba too much after…

70.t: Pops Foster, first string bassist in jazz
70.s: Jackson says Pops Foster brought the string bass to New York with Luis Russell, with Hinton noting Bill Johnson in Chicago.
70.ch: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
70.q: Pops Foster, that played with Lu Russell. He was playing with Lu Russell when Red Allen and Higginbotham and all those guys were in the band then.

70.s: Pettiford hung out backstage with Hinton, nearly got Hinton fired by Calloway, and briefly filled in with Ellington after Blanton.
70.ch: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
70.q: I worked with him in Ellington's band and when I worked with him there I'll never forget him. He just worked there a little while while I was there. He come in, you know, in Wendell's place. When Wendell left the band, he come in and worked in there a little while and he didn't want to travel too…

70.t: Wellman Braud and Billy Taylor in Ellington's band
70.s: Jackson explains Braud was soon forgotten after Billy Taylor arrived, and Taylor quit when Blanton came.
70.ch: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
70.q: Oh, yeah, because they was there together and Freddie Guy, you know. They would talk about him but you never heard too much -- Duke would mention his name now and then -- but you never heard too much about him, because after Billy Taylor came in his place they forgot about him.

70.s: Hinton and Jackson recall Alsbrook, a brilliant bassist, cellist and arranger who studied at Minnesota, had sleeping sickness and was a Golden Gloves boxer.
70.ch: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
70.q: He was going to the University of Minnesota and he used to astound the teachers out there. He used to tell them things, you know.

70.s: Jackson praises Richard Davis's bowing that makes the bass sound like a cello.
70.ch: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
70.q: He could take a bow and make a bow play so -- he could take a bow just like, to me, the greatest guy I know today -- all due respects to you because you know I love you -- but, to me, I can listen to Richard Davis take a bow --

70.s: Both bassists played with Chick Webb; Beverly Peer, from Boston, now plays with Bobby Short at the Carlyle.
70.ch: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
70.q: Yes, he played with Chick Webb. -- a very good bass player and a very good foundation bass player. And, also, the bass player that followed him, to me, was a very good bass player. And right today he is playing at the Carlisle with --

70.t: Dud Bascomb's son on Fender bass
70.s: Bascomb's son is a fine New York bassist with a Fender; like father, like son.
70.ch: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
70.q: Yeah, I've worked with him and he's something else with that Fender bass, gee whiz.

70.s: Wendell Marshall, Blanton's cousin, lived in Jimmy's shadow, guarded his health, left Fiddler on the Roof to become a minister, and was a perfect gentleman.
70.ch: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
70.q: Wendell was a very good bass player but he's lived in Jimmy's shadow because it was his cousin. Blanton was -- I mean, Wendell wasn't what you would call a real heavy bass player but you could feel him. You would know he was there and he did the best, he tried to do the best he could and he…

70.t: Junior Raglin and Jimmy Woode joining Ellington
70.s: Junior Raglin was a lovable drinker who played guitar before bass; when he had to leave, Duke tried out Jimmy Woode in Boston.
70.ch: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
70.q: Because, you see, Blanton and them -- he and Blanton played together before Duke got him when he was playing guitar and Blanton was playing bass. --

70.t: Montgomery Morrison and Billy Taylor, tuba and bass players
70.s: His first great bass player was Montgomery Morrison on upright tuba in Zack White's band; then Billy Taylor in McKinney's.
70.ch: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
70.q: He used to take a tuba, an upright tuba and stand up with it and hold it like this and bounce and play. He could swing you to death. His name was Montgomery Morrison.

168.t: Comedy versus music, and bass solos in the 1930s
168.s: Stewart insists he was serious about his music; he was already featured as a bowed and humming soloist before meeting Slim.
168.q: Yes, I was very serious about my music, you know, and as a matter of fact, I did quite a bit of bowing and humming along with our act, you know. And I, as time went on, you know, I was still searching for better sounds with my solos and, you know.

168.t: Bowed bass solos as a novelty; Slim and Slam ends in 1941
168.s: Bowing was almost unheard of in jazz bass then; Stewart popularized bowed solos and bassists like John Kirby were fascinated. The duo lasted until Slim was drafted in 1941.
168.q: No, there wasn't very much. At times on slow numbers there was, they would bow straight notes, you know, not solo-wise. They would just be bowing the fundamental bass notes, you know, to the music, of course, whatever they were playing. And that's about the only time they would be bowing, which was…

168.t: Major Holley takes up the bow and sings with his bass
168.s: Few bassists took up the bow after him, but Major Holley, a friend since the late '30s, tried to outdo him, singing in his bass register.
168.q: Well, the fellows mostly continued to play, playing pizzicato. Maybe one or two bassists started using the bow after I had started, say like Major Holly. There's quite a story about old Major. We were the greatest of friends, of course, but Major told me during that time --

168.t: Which bassists had the biggest sound
168.s: Walter Page had an immense sound; others named are Hinton, Blanton, Pettiford and Braud.
168.q: Heavy, real heavy, and that's what a bass -- a bass needs, you know, is that sound, depth.

168.s: He met no classical bassists in England or during the Tatum years, but Koussevitzky, whom he met briefly in Boston, thought him among the best in jazz around 1938.
168.q: Well, I met some of the people who came to visit while I was working with Tatum, but I never did meet any classical bassists.

168.t: How he extended the bass range, working on it since 1937
168.s: He began developing high notes around 1937, inspired by Ray Perry's violin, and keeps the method secret; he adds comedy at the end.
168.q: That's where I really actually -- it came to me all of a sudden. "Why can't I make my fiddle sound, my bass fiddle, sound like a little violin?" It was one of those spur of the moment thoughts that I came across. So I tried to -- eventually I figured out a way to make these high notes on my bass…

168.t: Playing Play, Fiddle, Play and the conventional highest bass notes
168.s: After an on-tape performance, Stewart says conventional bass stopped near G because higher sounds like a cello, so the high notes were his gimmick.
168.q: Okay. (Singing), Please excuse me and forgive me. Please help me, we'll try to do better next time to reach that high note. When we try to play, play fiddle, play fiddle, play.

168.t: High action among the great bassists
168.s: Stewart always played with high action; he recalls that Braud, Blanton, Pettiford and Page did too, giving a big sound.
168.q: Walter Page? Yes, ... comes back to me as time goes by, yes, and we think about those days.

168.t: Playing two basses with Jimmy Blanton
168.s: At the party Blanton and Stewart played together with similar styles; Blanton played only pizzicato while Stewart used the bow.
168.ch: Movies and the Los Angeles scene
168.q: We were somewhat alike in our styles, you know, and what I mean is -- it's hard to explain, But I will say that Jimmy, Jimmy Blanton was a wonderful bassist.

168.s: Stewart uses the classical position but gets vibrato or tremolo with two fingers, one fixed and one shaking, a style of his own.
168.ch: Boston, Buffalo and finding a style
168.q: Classical position mostly. At times -- I have developed a way to play as I feel, what would you say, non-orthodox.

168.t: Right-hand fingering and the two-finger tremolo demonstrated
168.s: He shows plucking with both fingers or one finger braced on the thumb, and the tremolo with first and second fingers on Tenderly.
168.q: Yeah. (Playing bass.) Wait a minute, no. I'm playing the wrong thing. Let's do this one. (Playing bass.) You get the tremolo on that? (Singing)..... Tenderly.

168.t: Using several fingers for a strong low note on gut strings
168.s: With high action and gut strings he stacks three fingers behind the note for strength, both arco and pizzicato.
168.q: Yes. Well, in other words, if I were to make a note, so-called legitimately, like a B-flat, with my little finger, in some cases, I use all of my -- more or less put three fingers along with it and a couple of other fingers along with my little finger in order to give it more strength because of…

8.t: How pizzicato and slap bass came about
8.s: He says nobody knew who first plucked; players broke bows, picked, and slap bass developed from that.
8.q: Well, all I can tell you, I don't know who was the first to pick. It looked like it's just one of them things that looked like it just come up to all of us. See, from the pizzicata, you know.

8.s: He describes slapping the strings against the fingerboard, which does not suit records.
8.q: Cause it makes too much noise. You understand. slap your fingerboard hitting it. Pap, pap, pap. No, I'm fine. No, I don't hit the fingerboard at all, no. You get a true tone out of your enderman.

8.s: He practiced scales and solos, including Holy City and Walk With Me, bowed.
8.q: Scales. Yeah, I used to practice, I tell you a lot of things I used to practice. I used to practice a lot of solos. I liked solos.

8.s: He says he uses French style bow grip.
8.q: See, yeah, that's it. I think they bow like the German style. French style. French style. French style.

8.s: He dislikes aluminum basses; his own Swiss-made bass was bought in Los Angeles around 1921.
8.q: No, I played on those. I don't want one. No, they ain't no good. You don't like the tone? Ain't nobody. It's how long they last. They don't last, do you? You crack them or not crack them, down them, you understand? And no tone out of them.

8.t: The fourth string on the bass and Henry Kimball
8.s: Whether basses always had a fourth string, and Henry Kimball making Garland put one on and showing him fingering.
8.ch: New Orleans bands, brass bands and learning bass
8.q: Well, as far as I know, they always have fourth strings. They always have? Up to mine. But I used to, most of the boys used to take the E string off. Uh huh. Because the finger though, fourth string, most of the, I was playing, I was playing fourth strings, was, I was playing in the theater and the…

8.t: Slap bass and why he gave it up
8.s: He brought slap bass from New Orleans to Chicago and California but stopped because it wore grooves in fingerboards and made no notes.
8.q: I finally done that, you understand. I used to have this slap bass business. (Imitating sound of slapping bass fiddle.) I brought that back to Chicago from New Orleans, you know, that slap bass.

8.t: Johnny Lindsay and the Morgan family of bassists
8.s: Garland recalls bassist Johnny Lindsay and the Morgans from St. John the Baptist Parish, including Al Morgan.
8.q: Well all those -- all those Morgans was all right. All the Morgan -- the one who played saxophone, that's the last one died.

8.s: He names Sam Nixon, Henry Kimball and Jimmy Brown as good bassists.
8.q: Well, it was, oh, we had, let me see, Sam. Sam Nixon. Huh? Sam Nixon. Sam Nixon. Sam Nixon was a pretty good bass player. Yeah. Oak Gospel. Yeah. Well, my bass to leave for as far as I, in my book was, Henry Kimball was Thompson. See? Well, he was an actor, good musician, reason everything, you…

8.t: Other bassists: Slam Stewart, Blanton, Arvell Shaw
8.s: Garland likes Slam Stewart and Arvell Shaw.

635.s: Foster picks with the first two fingers together for volume and grips the strings for tone.

635.s: The range of strings and pedal notes on his four-string bass, why high C strings lose bass volume, and five-string basses.

635.s: Foster had the first metal bass and discusses tone, flat-back basses and putting a mic on the bass.
635.q: Wait a minute. Where's that big picture? See that big picture there? Show you the aluminum base. I had the first gold one. No, no, no, no, that one. The one with the whole band on it. Oh, yeah.

635.q: Three-legged, yeah. I was going to try to look at it more the other night. Do you like it all right? Yeah, it gives it a bigger tone.

635.t: Bass placement on the bandstand and the f-hole
635.s: Why Foster stands on a certain side of the band so the bass sound carries.
635.q: See, your F-hole was on the string bass, but it's into the band, not away from the band. Right. The F-hole. Now, you play with them bands, the bass, but not the ball. See, the only way a bass player on the opposite side of the stand, that's the only place where you got room to play.

635.t: Who first picked the string bass; Foster's bass in Los Angeles and New York

635.ch: New Orleans bands, players and halls

635.t: First three-string basses and who had four strings
635.s: Foster recalls early New Orleans bassists having three-string basses, with Jimmy Brown the one with four.
635.q: Three. Very few guys had full string basses. I remember around the North, all of them had three string basses. 243.t: Electric basses, five-string basses and wanting a full-size bass
243.s: Breaux dislikes electric bass, tried a five-string, notes the E string was removed on some basses, and still wants a full-size bass.
243.q: Yeah I tried that. I played on it but I mean I never used it for my personal stuff. A lot of the bells around here was taken off the E string. Because the E string is so deep. And it's not too very effective. Especially with the.

243.t: Playing heavy, soft-touch bassists and plywood basses
243.s: He says he plays loud and heavy, names soft players who use amplifiers, and compares carved wood basses with plywood ones.
243.q: Well, I actually work hard. I just, I mean, I always did play a heavy bass. Always did. I don't say I always played exactly right, but I always did play loud and real heavy.

243.t: Bass players Breaux admired: Albert Morgan, Blanton, Kid Twat, Chester, Cleo
243.s: Breaux names the New Orleans and other bassists he liked when young, from Albert Morgan and Jimmy Blanton to Kid Twat, Chester and Cleo.
243.q: name in the background and you remember well i liked that uh albert morgan was real nice he suited matthias wellman albert morgan and uh there's another youngster that started but he died young he got in duke's band after wellman left jimmy blannon blannon blannon that's his name he was a very fine…

248.s: Dawson claims to have started the four-four picked rhythm; bows suit waltzes and vocal numbers.

248.s: Dawson says he started the four-four rhythm on bass, used a bow for sentimental pieces and plucked for Dixieland, and praises Pickaninny who did both.
248.ch: String bands, serenading and violin players
248.q: Well, who did? In fact, I, I'm the one who started that four-four rhythm with one thing. Uh-huh. You used to play with a bow too? Yeah. I was my main out with a bow. Yeah.

248.s: Garland explains rehairing a bow with black thread, rosin and ceiling wax, and tells of replacing a broken G-string with twine.

And the lady out there that was running Lincoln Beach, she stood for security for that bass. He bought that bass…

248.t: Charlie Galloway, the one-legged bass player
248.s: Galloway played bowed bass with a crutch, known as Happy or Lovin' Galloway.
248.q: You say he was a one-legged man? One leg, yeah. He had a stick. He had a stick, a kind of a crutch, you know. He used to support his stuff with that bad leg, you know. And he could carry that bass. Them times you carry the bass on your back with a strap, you see. Yeah. He could really get around…

248.t: Dawson's claim to start picking the bass; other early bassists
248.s: Dawson says he started four-four finger picking, which Pop Foster and others followed; remembers Jimmy Johnson and Jimmy Brown.
248.q: I started Pop Foster, and he'll tell you he's living the day. I started with that one finger, picking that four-four rhythm. And from that on, they start making that four-four rhythm, you know, picking with one finger like that. You put the bow down. And they just went right on up. And when I…
