877.t: Credit, pride and buying a bass through Beansie
877.s: Handy tells how he refused credit out of pride, then chose a bass costing about $390 and Beansie paid $100 down.
877.q: Well, they had one for, they had several cheap basses. Well, a big three-quarter bass like I was telling you about the fella had over home. But I didn't like that. I was kind of concerned about a small bass. It's right there, right now. Right back here. Right back here. It's back there in the…

877.s: Handy plays the bass left-handed with no changes to the instrument, because he learned on Selby Thomas's violin; he cannot play Kimball's left-strung bass.
877.q: Nothing changed. Just like a right-hand man, I can get up. Now, Kimball bass, I can't play yet. It's strung up left-handed.

877.s: Handy bowed and plucked at first; he thinks bowing carries slow numbers better, but bowing has largely disappeared except in large orchestras.
877.q: No, they don't bow very little. You catch the best of the violin playing, the biggest instrument, biggest band in here. They have bowing where they have a whole lot of cellars. They have bowing with beats, but outside of that, you don't catch that anymore. It's all picking. All picking. So, there…

877.t: Carrying the bass; folding basses and bass guitars
877.s: The bass is an awkward instrument, once needing a City Hall pass on streetcars; Handy would like a folding bass but dislikes bass guitars.
877.q: That's when I want to stop and get a sandwich or something to bring home that I have to lock the car up and I still go backwards and find to see if someone's trying to break in the car to take it out. You understand? It's an awkward thing to carry. It is. You take like that and drums, they're…

454.t: Bass battles and the best he ever played
454.s: He names a San Francisco jam session as his best; Blanton, Slam Stewart and Callender left no competition.
454.ch: Second interview: bass, Parker and Miles
454.q: Well, the best I ever played was Oscar came to San Francisco with Duke and Vern Ellis (inaudible) jam session.

454.t: Why Jimmy Blanton mattered, and jazz bass versus classical bass
454.s: Blanton played high and low in all keys, unlike Walter Page; a story of a bass player who could not sight-read; classical bass soloists seem simple by comparison.
454.ch: Second interview: bass, Parker and Miles
454.q: Well, a lot of guys -- see, like, Eddie Gomez, they can (inaudible), but they don't. They only play up high. Some musicians (inaudible), but Jimmy Blanton played up high and down low, (inaudible).

454.s: Mingus likes Gomez but wishes he would use the whole bass.
454.ch: Kid Ory, Hampton, Ellington and Ben Webster
454.q: He plays a tune, and he's very fast. But I can't see why he doesn't use the full -- uses the bass, top and bottom. If he'd do that, he'd cut everybody. Right now, he's just playing high.

454.t: Where the next improviser comes from; Scott LaFaro at the Showplace
454.s: LaFaro slept in a chair at the Showplace; Mingus thinks he started bass playing for its own sake.
454.ch: Ellington, singers, the book and closing
454.q: But it might come from some little cat like Lafaro was. Scott Lafaro used to come to my job at the Showplace, put his feet up on a chair and go to sleep, every night. Matter of fact, the date I did with you, --

454.t: Ray Brown, Red Mitchell and melodic bass playing
454.s: Brown played exercises; Red Mitchell is the only bassist who plays melodically.
454.ch: Ellington, singers, the book and closing
454.q: Composition. Anybody can take a bass and say (singing). Go up and down, playing scales (inaudible). I was surprised to hear Ray do that.

454.t: Retyped pages: bass battles and Jimmy Blanton
454.s: Repeat of the talk on bass contests and Blanton's technique.
454.q: Well, a lot of guys -- see, like, Eddie Gomez, they can (inaudible), but they don't. They only play up high. Some musicians (inaudible), but Jimmy Blanton played up high and down low, (inaudible).

259.t: Sorting out bassists Eddie Dorsey and Eddie Jackson
259.s: A back-and-forth to establish which long-tall bass player Eddie is; Jackson dead, Dorsey alive.
259.q: Yeah, he used to play with that. You know what I'm talking about? Eddie Dorsey? Yeah, he used to play with bass player. I used to play with him sometimes too, you know. With who? With a different band. Long Tall Dock.

259.t: Good bass players and Snags Jones
259.s: He names bass players (Fulston, Scott, T-Boy) and discusses drummer Clifford Jones, known as Snag.
259.q: He said, how about some of the good bass players? Well, George Fulston, he was good. Eddie Scott, Lil Chester. Yeah, what called Lil Chester? He's down there, yep. I see them, but...

259.t: Hats and Coats and bassist Liberty Newton
259.s: Allen asks about the one-legged Hats and Coats; Vincent offers the washtub player and then Liberty Newton, a bass player who worked with MS Lawyers.
259.q: So you know Hats and Coats, the one-legged fellow? Coat. Hats and Coke. Hats and Coats. Hats and Coats.

259.t: Where Mutt Carey went; Eddie Gordon on bass
259.s: Mutt Carey left for California; Vincent recalls bassist Eddie Gordon.
259.q: Where did Mutt Carey go when he left Jack? He was in Chicago, California. Went back over there. I think he come back here and died, I think. Know he died up there? California. Oh yeah, that's right, yeah. He was with the kid over there, I think. You know Eddie Gordon, didn't he? He was a good…

259.t: Wellman Braud, his sweepstake win, and the record date with Edmund Hall
259.s: Vincent describes bassist Wellman Braud, who won a large sweepstake and opened a restaurant, and the recording session where Braud could not return and George Foster played bass.
259.q: He said, why did you know Wilman Bro? Wilman Bro? Wilman Bro, he came from Central 5. He used to play with us, you know, with three and four piece bands. He never played with no big bands. He was a good bass player. Ask him what else for him. He used to play tambour and cornet and violin. He got a…

456.t: Three-string basses in Italy and the low C extension
456.s: His Italian teacher's bass had three strings, as in Bottesini's day; the E string came later, and a lever mechanism extends it to low C for Strauss and Prokofiev.
456.q: Oh yeah, yeah. In fact, that's all there was. My teacher had a three-string bass in Italy, and that's all there was. In the, in the years of the famous bass player Giovanni Bottezzini, they just had G, D and A, and A was the lowest string in the bass. And it was only recently, I'd say about, ooh,…

456.s: Best practice is thumb on the fingerboard and alternating two fingers; he warns against fakers and describes slap bass as a percussive style gone out of fashion.
456.q: Well, everybody has his own style of how to hold their fingers, you know. A lot of guys just use one finger, a lot of guys use two. Of course, the best way is to put your thumb on the fingerboard, and you get a good leverage that way. And you use two fingers, the index and what you call this finger…

456.t: Bowing in jazz and Slam Stewart
456.s: Jazz bassists are now expected to bow a chorus; Mazzari recalls being scorned for it years ago and notes today's bowers do not simply imitate Slam Stewart.
456.q: And in those days, I think that they were just saying, well, man, who do you think you are imitating Slam Stewart? Like, so these guys today, they're imitating Slam Stewart? No, they don't sound at all like Slam Stewart. They have their own individual way of playing. So I'm glad to see that. I…

456.s: American players split about 50-50; he would mix both bows in a symphony section for their different strengths, and himself uses the German bow.
456.q: Oh, either way, you can... There is a... I would say it's a 50-50 proposition in this country. It's about 50% play French bow, 50% play German bow. And I tell you, if I were a conductor in the symphony orchestra, I would try to have a French bow and a German bow divided into each stand, because…

456.t: Pizzicato technique: symphony versus jazz bassists
456.s: Mazzari explains good hand and thumb position, how to tell trained from untrained bassists, and praises Bob Ciccarelli, who plays everything in position.
456.q: Well, uh, any good, uh, symphony bass player will play pizzicato properly and it's very easy to see why the, why the bass player is holding, is doing it. I mean, uh...

1.t: New Orleans bassists Pops Foster and Wellman Braud in New York
1.s: Few New Orleans players were in New York, but Al Morgan, Pops Foster and Wellman Braud brought slap bass, while Harlem's clubs and ethnic bars are described.
1.q: There weren’t that many. The ones who were there, they were working with bands. I was the only one out there by myself. All the musicians was mad about New Orleans musicians, because they were innovators. Al Morgan come in. The first day he was there. Next day he was with the McKinney’s Cotton…

1.t: Braud and Foster's bass playing and fingers taped against blisters
1.s: Braud pulled Ellington's band with his bass, Foster did the same for Russell, and bassists taped fingers before amplification.
1.q: Yeah, The Mooche, but them fast movement. St. Louis Toodle-oo and them kind of things. You hear Braud. He’s just a musician. You can dig that. He just take that tempo where he feel it should go. Duke didn’t mind, because there was energy given, and it made his band swing, that had never swung…

1.s: Danny and Milt recall the Pettiford family and Adolphus Allsbrook, a bass-playing trombonist and judo expert who wrote for Lawrence Welk.
1.ch: Danny's rise through New York bands to Cab Calloway
1.q: and you... You go to Detroit. There's a whole bunch of musicians there that's got a cult going, and they're playing up there. You'd go to Minneapolis, there are some musicians there, them Pettiford Brothers, the Pettiford family. Adolphus...

1.t: Harry White has Simon Marrero sent for from New Orleans
1.s: Harry White wanted a bassist like Albert Morgan or Pops Foster, so Danny and Paul sent for Simon Marrero, who got off in Newark by mistake.
1.ch: Arriving in New York: the Nest Club and Harlem nightlife
1.q: Harry was a wonderful musician. He was an arranger. He arranged some things that Duke used. And he and I... He just liked me. So later on he asked me... Albert Morgan had come through and made a splash on the bass, and Pops Foster was with Luis Russell, and everybody was taking lessons from him.…

1.t: Simon Marrero wins the Rhythm Club bass contest and McKinney's offer
1.s: Simon's finger-style bass amazed the Rhythm Club, and McKinney offered him a job in Detroit, while Goldie was sent for to keep him in New York.
1.ch: Arriving in New York: the Nest Club and Harlem nightlife
1.q: So... Yeah, that's right. So we fooled together... I mean, we were close together, now, and he comes to the house. He goes around to the Rhythm Club every day, because everything was centered around there. And McKinney's Cotton Pickers are in town playing some New England dates. So they got him…

380.t: His first bass solo on Gerald Wilson's "Dissonance in Blues"
380.s: He says the feature was written for him and a bootleg credited the wrong player.
380.q: Yeah. It was "Dissonance in Blues," an original that Gerald wrote especially to feature me on the bass. I saw it lately. Some bootleggers in Europe or somewhere had copied the record, and they didn't know who the bass player was, so they just inserted some name. But for posterity and everything,…

380.t: Hearing Jimmy Blanton and playing pizzicato solos
380.s: He says Blanton showed how the bass should be played, unlike Slam Stewart's bowing, and that he followed him around.
380.q: Well, I used to play solos, you know, mostly melodic solos. But the most impressive bass player that I heard has to be Jimmy Blanton.

380.t: Jimmy Blanton's inspiration, sound and technique
380.s: They discuss Blanton's violin background and cousin Wendell Marshall, and Callender praises his force and big sound.
380.q: Hmm, well. Anyhow, he was a good bass player, too, but not of the same caliber as Blanton. Blanton was very forceful, and what a big sound, and what technique, and what beautiful fingers. He seemed to be able to pick up any instrument and really play it -- any bass, that is. That's something that a…

380.t: His basses: the Morellis, Mingus's Roth and Uly Apfell
380.s: He tells how salesman Uly Apfell sold him the Morelli bass he bought for the Armstrong job, and about the others he owns.
380.ch: Films, Las Vegas and the union
380.q: At least. I got a letter from his estate attorney, and it was a big surprise: "Charles Mingus has willed his Roth bass to one Red Callender." So I went to New York and checked it out, and I brought it back. It was just that simple.

380.t: Rock-and-roll dates and playing the Fender bass
380.s: He recalls the Fender bass overpowering the upright on dates, his work on Flip Wilson and Carol Burnett, and a Frank De Vol call for all three basses.
380.q: Like, I've done some record dates that were pretty dumb here and there. But even then, you realize that no matter how dumb a thing is at the moment, it only lasts for a few hours. So you can live through anything. And I was in the beginning of I guess you'd call the Rock-and-Roll scene, and even…

251.t: A showman bassist who spun and slapped the bass
251.s: Albert describes a bassist who rode, spun and slapped his instrument for show, and how musicians cite small hometowns.
251.q: band. Yeah, I saw a letter from drinks, he started to buy a lot of people, and they were like, they were like, oh, I'm not a big fan of the band. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm.

251.t: Bassist Jimmy Johnson, string bass and drums
251.s: Jimmy Johnson was an old but strong ear player; the band was among the first to use string bass, adding Harold Holmes. Talk drifts to his bicycle and a drummer's plain drum set.
251.q: Sure he was. He was in beautiful health. He was a strong old man. And he still drank his whiskey, but he never was drunk on the job that I can remember. But Jimmy was strong, as strong as anyone in the band had to be to play the way he played. See, my band is one of the first bands to use a string…

251.t: String bass versus tubas in Texas and New Orleans
251.s: Albert brought Jimmy Johnson's string bass from New Orleans to Texas, where bands used tubas; recalls recruiting him on Annunciation Street in 1929.
251.q: Mine was, well, you had this fella that was originally from Louisiana. They called him Manoon. I was living in Houston outside, but he wasn't playing too much. But, I brought Jimmy. He left here with me. And, that was the first time they had ever seen a string bass in a band. It was a novelty to…

251.t: Basses in Albert's band: Nick Turner, Jimmy Johnson, Harold Holmes
251.s: Turner played tuba and valve trombone; the band used three basses.
251.q: First band, they used three basses. You had three basses? Two string basses and Nick on the tuba. Who were the string basses? Uh, old man, uh, Jimmy Johnson. Uh-huh. Uh, Harold Holmes. And Nick Turner. Where? First band to use the word swing.

264.t: Playing the bow and three-quarter bass
264.s: Zardis explains he used the bow only on waltzes and soft numbers, otherwise plucked, and his hand position in the photo.
264.ch: Technique and the Covington band's sound
264.q: Did you use it most of the time? No, on the bows we used to just have occasionally like, you know what I mean? It wasn't regular because the bow didn't go with that jazz music unless you got a soft number. Like a waltz or shardis. Well that's when you use that bow. I was telling that bow every day…

264.t: Three-string versus four-string bass, bass horn and the jitney dance
264.s: Zardis explains why a three-string bass hampered reading music, mentions playing bass horn and a jitney dance with Petit.
264.ch: Technique and the Covington band's sound
264.q: Well I'll tell you, I bought a bass with the same bass I tell you about with the old man. Well he had three strings on that bass. Bill and Moran. Yeah, Bill and Moran. Well after that third, that fourth string, I go to make a G, like sometimes I'm playing a soft number and I have my bow and I will…

264.t: Three-string basses and how they were tuned
264.s: Many bassists used three strings; Zardis explains the straight E, A, D, G tuning.
264.q: No, no, no, no, no, no. You're talking about like ukulele, it's like. No, no, no, straight, just straight. E, A, D, G. Yeah, straight.

264.t: Other early string bass players and Coochie Morton, Kimball and Glennie
264.s: Zardis names earlier bassists such as Johnny Lindsey, Pop Foster, Albert Glennie and Cleo, and recalls Henry Kimball teaching him.
264.q: Well I'll tell you who was good, you take this old boy, I forget his name. He died a good while back. But Johnny was a good boy. Johnny played a whole lot of bass. Johnny what was his name? Johnny Lindsey. Oh Johnny Lindsey, yeah. And you take Pop Foster, he was in that one. He was around there,…

13.t: Jimmy Blanton, Oscar Pettiford and the bass becoming a solo instrument
13.s: Bass had been a section instrument.
13.q: I remember him in Kansas City. Jimmy Blanton, and there was -- I'm trying to think of this bass player, well, outside of Oscar Pettiford in Minneapolis. He was another one.

Well, not exactly. Other than tried to get some solos together myself, you know what I mean. Listen to him, and watching his fingering, and everything, well, being an ex-violin player, it came easy to me, you know. All I had to do was just get my ideas together.

13.t: Joining Hines in place of Hayes Alvis and doubling
13.s: He joined an established band on string bass and tuba and preferred tuba at first.
13.ch: Joining Earl Hines and the Grand Terrace
13.q: At that time I liked the tuba better than the string bass, because string bass was kind of rough for me back in them days, you know. It takes years and years to perfect -- to get the perfection on the string bass, and then
Unless I could pick up by ear, you know, like I'd say Jimmy Blanton, Ray Brown, just by listen- int to different bass players.

764.t: Slap bass technique and the scarred Rittner bass
764.s: Manno explains how Charlie Rittner's habit of striking the bass with the bow led to slapping and pulling the strings, and how the hand moves.
764.q: oh well that that's quite a story because this bass that I have back in Houston is a French instrument it's quite a famous instrument it's a GAN and I got the instrument from a man by the name of Eugene Deal who had bought the instrument from Charlie Rittner who uh had played in the theater and one…

764.t: Bass-knob picking, Banuelas's rubber hose act and Rittner in the theaters
764.s: Manno has never heard of picking with the bow knob; he describes a Texas bassist who slapped with a rubber hose in a sombrero act, and Rittner's theater work.
764.q: uh in fact that's the first time i've ever heard that mentioned in fact i couldn't think of anything more awkward to do it it sounds awkward to me uh now i'll tell you what what they did over there now uh there was uh a man over there by the name of uh Antonio Banyuelas who used to slap the base…

764.t: The Gann bass and Manno's Esquire mention
764.s: Photo of the bass is requested; Manno describes the half-size French Gann bass and its scars from Rittner's bow strikes.
764.q: just just an individual yes mm-hmm now you're saying about that bass you got from Charlie Rittner oh well I got it's it's a half-size bass and it was made by Gann who was a violin maker in Miracourt and he also states that he got the wood for this particular instrument out of the was it Vorgias…

569.t: Jimmy Johnson, Bob Lyons, and a gap in playing
569.s: He remembers other bassists, recalls following Newton around, and says he stopped playing for twelve to fifteen years.
569.q: Oh, well I don't know, I can't recall who he was playing with at the time, cause I was kind of young you know, and I used to go around. When I used to go to these places I went with Liv, Liv Newton. You know, he carried me around everywhere he played, that's how I come to start the playing bass.…

569.t: Early bass players: Data Jackson, Henry Kimball, Bebe Ridgley
569.s: He remembers Data Jackson, who played bass fiddle before tuba, and Henry Kimball playing with Bebe Ridgley.
569.q: Jackson, yeah. Data Jackson. Data Jackson, yeah. He used to play bass fiddle too. At the time when I started playing, trying to play bass. He was playing string bass then, he wouldn't play in tuba. Is that right? Oh sure, he started playing tuba after, way after that. I didn't know. He did, yeah.

569.t: Chester Zardis as model; his bass technique and instrument
569.s: He names Chester Zardis as his model and compares him with Newton, then discusses slapping, strings and his German basses.
569.q: That's right. He's about the, he's about the, I would say, about the hardest working boy that I saw play bass. He's just about the hardest worker. I wouldn't say he the best, but that's the one I prefer. That's the one you like. And I play his own order, him, because he showed me the swing. Yeah.…

45.t: Reel three begins; bass in Ridgely's band at Suburban Gardens
45.s: Williams names bassists he worked with in Ridgely's band, who played at Suburban Gardens in 1928.
45.q: Yeah, I'm not sure. Shots was with him a lot. Handy. Sills. David Jones. Mm-hmm. We played out the Suburban Garden. I was playing bass. Played out the Suburban Garden in 1928. Something else I wanted to ask you about.

45.t: Bass players Vic Gaspar, Albert Glenny and Buddy Johnson
45.s: Williams recalls which bands bass players such as Glenny and Johnson played in.
45.q: Before he'd come on the roof cart with us. You know. Jimmy. Jimmy. Huh? The bass player you're talking about. No, Buddy Johnson. Yank's brother. He was on the roof cart. He was on the roof cart. Yeah. Yeah. That was swell. That was swell.

45.t: Bowing the bass in the old bands
45.s: Williams says the bassists with Ridgely and others bowed their basses, which young players no longer do.
45.q: Oh, yeah, oh, yeah. Oh, you wasn't classy, no bass player. Man, bow your bass. These youngsters just picked the bass. They can't even use a bow. Oh, the bow's just like for a violin, a smaller violin.

681.t: Ellis Stratakos's band and three bass players who died
681.s: Hirsch played with Stratakos's group on the Gulf Coast; Ray Benitez, Frank Netto and Pat Easterling died recently.
681.ch: Gulf Coast and later working bands
681.q: Ellis was from the Gulf Coast. Yeah. It was Stranicos' man that we used to play over there with Charlie Wagner, Johnny Roniger, Meyer Weinberg, Doc Benitez. You know, he died recently. Oh, yes, he did, yeah. Doc died. Three bass players that worked with me the past 10 years. All died in a very…

681.t: Bass players: Netto's ear, Tony Lausa, Jack Abel
681.s: Hirsch talks about electric and upright bass players, Frank Netto's perfect ear, and bassists who cannot play the changes.
681.ch: Music in the family, learning to play
681.q: I never heard him play upright. He was playing electric. It might have been Tim Jackson. I don't know but he was good. He was here in town. But he plays upright.

681.t: Slim Lamar and Ray Bonitas becoming a bass player
681.s: Hirsch recalls the band that went to Jackson, Mississippi with a Conn sales manager, where he moved from piano to drums and Ray Bonitas was made a bass player.
681.q: Well, that was the first band that was over there. I know it was a long time ago. And, uh... It was... I don't know who the hell was the leader of it. I think it was Ellis Straticus. I'm not sure. But then later, I found a name of... Johnny, uh... He was a sales manager for CG Khan. He said, well,…

831.t: String bass, sousaphone and upright bass horns early on
831.s: He explains that early bands used string bass, with a few upright bass horns rather than sousaphones.
831.q: Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. They had bass horns at times. Uh huh. They didn't call them sousaphone. They had upright bass horns.

831.t: Mario Fanats, the best bass player
831.s: He praises Fanats, a big man whose upright horn sounded like a bass fiddle, and talks about his sons.
831.q: Yeah. Yeah. Well, Fanats was a big heavy set man himself. Uh huh. But he blew a sousaphone and it sounded like a bass fiddle. Right. But he not a sousaphone but upright bass. It sounded just like a, man I remember one night, he come and we had a four piece job. In a house, a house party. And they…

831.t: Steve Brown and slap bass technique
831.s: He praises Steve Brown and explains slapping bass strings against the fingerboard, like a wood block.
831.q: thumb back against that backboard or tail the thumb against the headboard that way and i picked this way away from the string i never picked i never picked the strings out with a slap back well who featured that slap back in the old oh god most everybody that played bass played that's what we call…

801.s: How older bassists bowed and plucked with two fingers, got calluses, preferred four strings, and learned chords.
801.q: Or you take a number when it first, you first, well most of the bands in those days didn't play the introduction of a number because half of them couldn't read good enough to do it. And the bands wasn't qualified enough to do it. But they was fab musicians. Yeah, they really played what they could…

801.t: Jimmy Brown, Old Man Kimball and Johnny Prudhomme
801.s: Eddie compares older bassists Jimmy Brown, Kimball and the rough-style Prudhomme with his father.
801.q: Yeah, and managing famous bands. Yeah. That's what made him... You know, but Jimmy Brown was a good-faced, bro. Extra good.

801.t: Other bassists: Jim Little and Albert Morgan
801.s: Eddie names Jim Little and Albert Morgan, whom Simon taught, and notes Sam Morgan's rule against letting others sit in.
801.q: Yeah, he was down here about two years ago. He's one of the youngest Morgan brothers. He'd come after all of them. Yeah.

58.t: Johnny Lindsay, Bill Matthews and others
58.s: They discuss the bass player's career and Matthews.
58.ch: Records, Jimmy Wade and Richard M. Jones
58.q: I didn't work with none, yeah. He played with Robichaud the whole time he was here. And let me see how he did that. Didn't he get off a bass on trombone or a trombone on bass or something? Yeah, that's right. Something like that, I remember.

58.t: Bass players, Johnny Lindsay, and New Orleans musicians who left young
58.s: Miller names New Orleans bassists, and they discuss Lindsay, Al Wynn and Simeon.
58.q: Simeon? The clarinet player. Yeah, I remember when he got, I don't know, he died, didn't he? Mm-hmm. Yeah.

58.t: How bass players got off: bowing and slapping; Louie Gallo
58.s: Miller describes a bassist who played with the end of the bow and a slap-style bassist on a record; they identify a pianist.
58.q: Well, tell me, one way I could say they could get off if the band makes stops like they do for trumpet, and the bass do all his work, and like we should do for Chester. We used to stop and he played all kind of bass. But he didn't, he played on front of bass. He didn't play with his fingers like…

328.s: Electric bass is audible but sits above the rhythm section; the upright blends.
328.q: When you use the electric bass, sometimes you don’t have any choice. The electric bass – the thing that’s good about the electric bass is that it’s very audible. You can hear it. You can make it heard on every note if you want to. But it takes away from the warmth of the feeling of the rhythm…

328.s: Hampton learned about other family bands later and praises Pettiford's role in bass literature.
328.ch: Practice, Indianapolis memories and the trombone
328.q: No, actually I became more aware of it later. When we were in the family band, we didn’t – we were in Indianapolis. So we didn’t have a lot of the news that was available to us. I learned later, after meeting Jimmy, and also, I didn’t meet him, but I heard Oscar Pettiford and several of the family…

328.s: Why he used tuba and euphonium and how tuba and acoustic bass pair, citing Miles Davis's Porgy and Bess.
328.q: The tuba fits into the foundation again. The tuba say, bawwww. You can write everything on top of that. It sounds wonderful, just from that one pedal point, because the tuba has always been – this has been the place of the tuba in all of music, the foundation. The euphonium is a small tuba. All…

686.t: How the 'without Bass Direct' joke began
686.s: Wynton's early bassists, Branford's Down Beat comments and a reader's reply led to the joke credit that caught on.
686.q: Ron Carter. No, he did his first CD with Ron Carter, and then I think Clarence Seay was on a song. At some point Ray Drummond played on the second recording. And Phil Bowler. He had a number of bassists. There was the concern of the lack of an acoustic sound, but also that that bass – it was…

686.t: Trio Jeepy with Milt Hinton changes bass recording
686.s: He steered Branford toward Ben Webster and Milt Hinton, and the resulting record showed what a recorded bass could sound like.
686.q: When we did Trio Jeepy, which was with Milt Hinton, which was again – it was my idea, that I would like to get the younger and the older musicians involved. I kept telling – when Branford was on the road with Sting, he would call me. “Man, this is like constant recess. I’m dying out here. It’s…

686.t: Bass today: musicians' balance and his advice to players
686.s: He says the improvement is in musicians' awareness, not technology, and urges students to develop their sound before plugging in.
686.q: No, it’s really more about the musicians understanding what they sound like, what the group sounds like. I think in a rock-and-roll situation, it’s almost loud, louder, loudest, and you just let the sound man deal with it. I think in an acoustic situation, it’s just like playing in an orchestra,…

26.t: Discovering Jimmy Blanton in St. Louis
26.s: Greer hears Blanton at a Fate Marable jam session and gets Duke to hire him for the Case Hotel.
26.q: Well, Jimmy Blanton, the first time I heard him was in St. Louis. We were in St. Louis to play the Case Hotel the first time they ever had a colored band. And so the night before -- we had two days off so the night before I went out on the town, and Fate Marable had a lot of very good musicians…

26.t: Why Blanton was different from other bass players
26.s: Greer says Blanton played horn solos on bass and inspired later bassists.
26.q: Old "Big'un", he's something else. But this guy, he started a brand new innovation for bass players when they heard him, you know. He was something, man.

26.t: Blanton versus Mingus and Ben Webster showing him off
26.s: Mingus said only Blanton beat him; Duke kept Blanton; Ben Webster took him out.
26.q: Jimmy'd eat him up, man. I'd play with both of them, Charlie and Jimmy. Eat them up, without any sweat. He was -- man, I don't know. He was so great. And when he was with us everybody tried to lure him. No chance. He's something else.

677.t: Finding Jimmy Blanton in St. Louis
677.s: Brown and Hodges heard Blanton in an after-hours place and brought him to Ellington at the Chase Hotel, where he was hired immediately.
677.ch: Ellington colleagues, singers and world tours
677.q: It was Johnny Hodges and I that went to that little cafe in St. Louis and brought Blanton to the Chase Hotel in St. Louis and we said, Ellington, listen to this fellow. And so he listened to him play a few

677.t: Blanton's tone and the microphone problem
677.s: Brown laments that early miking never captured Blanton's true tone and compares it to Ray Brown.
677.ch: Ellington colleagues, singers and world tours
677.q: Well he changed -- yes. It's too bad. I've always regretted that they never got the true tone with Blanton because in those days they didn't put the mike down near the soundpost in the bass fiddle. The mikes all were up in the air on the fingerboard, Well, if you know fingerboard is very tinny…

677.t: Blanton's influence and later Ellington bassists
677.s: Blanton, once a violinist, made the bass a solo instrument; Pettiford and Wendell Marshall followed.
677.ch: Ellington colleagues, singers and world tours
677.q: Well originally Jimmy Blanton was a violin player. And when you think of his playing, you would think more or less of a violin player doing what we call pluck -- plucking his instrument. And that's the way that he played only on the bass he plucked his bass and then he would turn around and bow --…

9.s: Neal was a bassist in taxi dance halls, and Pack was an altoist who left for Europe; Holmes never played with either.
9.q: Yeah, Bobby Neal was a... I think he was a bass player. He used to have a band around here. I can't tell you too much about him, because I never worked for him, but I knew people that did work for him.

9.t: Richard Fulbright, Edmond Hall and Cookie Mason of the Ross band
9.s: Holmes remembers Fulbright as a fine bassist, Hall as downtown-oriented, and Cookie Mason as a trumpeter he took for a gambler; touring bands faced jam sessions.
9.ch: Cass Carr, Crawley, Burnet and Cootie Williams
9.q: : Yeah, he played everything. He was very good. Uncle Dick, yeah. There's nothing more I can say about him. Just a good bass player, and some of them get breaks... He worked with quite a few bands. I can't remember whose bands he worked with...

9.t: Pops Foster's string bass changes New York bands
9.s: Only Ellington used string bass, with Wellman Braud, until Pops Foster's style spread; guitars were the last instrument bands hired.
9.ch: Harlem musicians and the road with Armstrong
9.q: : Well, when they had a bass, it was a string bass. In fact, Pops Foster changed the style in New York. See, they didn't change... See, Braud had been playing here for years, string bass, with Duke, and even before Duke. He didn't need nothin'. Soon as Pops Foster come around with the bass, then…

166.t: Stopping in St. Louis to hear Jimmy Blanton
166.s: On the way east he hears the astonishing Blanton, who played with Jeter-Pillars and studied under his violinist mother.
166.ch: Records, Blanton, the Chicago scene, Nat Cole and Nadine
166.q: Well, yes, well, it made me curious. Because I didn't know what I was doing. I said, well, people can see more in me than I can see in myself, you know? So I'll go back East where things are happening and just throw my hat in with the competition, and see what's being done and what has to be done.

166.t: Oscar Pettiford's playing, and taking Simmons's bass
166.s: Praise for Pettiford's solos with Duke and Hawkins; he twice took Simmons's bass overnight.
166.q: Now I remember a record that he made with Duke that just gassed me, 'Airconditioned Jungle'. Jimmy Hamilton had the clarinet solo and Oscar played rhythm and melody right along with him, it was like a duet almost. He carried the melodic line and was playing the rhythm at the same time. And then…

166.t: Bassists Doug Watkins and Joe Benjamin, and Lena Horne
166.s: He acknowledges two solid bass players; Joe Benjamin was a copyist when Simmons worked for Lena Horne.
166.ch: Erroll Garner, the 1952 arrest and Florida
166.q: And other bass players that played unorthodox but still played in tune. And I left off a couple of bass players that I would like to acknowledge.

69.t: Bassists Hayes Alvis and Billy Taylor
69.s: Alvis was a showman, Taylor was straight and had a huge appetite.
69.q: Well, he was a showman on the bass. You know, hitting the things and all, and stuff like that. He was a good bass player, but he let the people see the way he was playing and so forth -- you know, hitting the thing and what not.

69.s: He heard Blanton play Sophisticated Lady with a bow in St. Louis and fetched Duke, who hired him.
69.q: Jimmy Blanton -- I went to see him, we was in St. Louis, and I went to see Jimmy Blanton once, because he was a fellow who used to take his bass and play with anybody, you know? In this particular cabaret, I went there and listened to him, and he was playing Sophisticated Lady with a bow, you know?…

69.s: Pettiford recorded Perdido on cello; Marshall ate raw potatoes and was Blanton's cousin.
69.q: He was another nice bass player, too. I don't know what kind of sickness he had, but the doctor used to tell him to eat raw potatoes. He would cut pieces of raw potatoes and eat it when he'd be at restuarants. I don't know what his trouble was.

428.t: First bass solos and showmanship with Bobby Booker's band
428.s: He took slapped solos on Claude Hopkins's theme, wearing a big red hat and spinning the bass, at the Club Harlem in 1934.
428.ch: Philadelphia bands and the Club Harlem
428.q: Yeah, I got solos. One of the first solos that I ever did was Claude Hopkin's theme song, 'I Could do Almost Anything For You.' And I used to wear a big red hat and straddle and slap and spin. This was show biz. If you didn't do that -- and I was an up and coming bass player at that time.

428.t: Great bass players: Blanton, Ray Brown and Pettiford
428.s: Hall's views on the bassists who changed the instrument and on Blanton and Christian dying young.
428.q: Jimmy Blanton changed the bass. Jimmy Blanton changed the whole concept of the bass. But I think the greatest bass player that I know is Ray Brown. He is complete in all aspects. I'm not putting down anybody else, but Ray Brown is --

428.t: Slapping and spinning the bass, and the older bassist's advice
428.s: Hall remembers Stanfield's style and Mr. Hayes telling him that spinning is not playing.
428.ch: Later life, World's Fair and Ellington
428.q: band come to the theater, and Stanfield was the bass player. And he was slapping and straddling and spinning it and whatnot.

78.t: Israel Crosby: a great bassist from Horace and Fletcher to Ahmad Jamal
78.s: Crosby played in Fletcher's Grand Terrace rhythm section, was loved by Billie Holiday and Hammond, recorded 'Flingin' a Whing Ding', and later played in Ahmad Jamal's strictly rehearsed trio.
78.ch: Portraits from Hemphill to Getz, and the bebop question
78.q: Huh! That's a coincidence. Well, Israel Crosby was one of the greatest bass players, not only in my estimation, but in the estimation of most of the musicians that heard him, really, one of the greatest bass players that ever played the bass. In fact, as small as the guy was, you know he could play…

78.t: Ahmad Jamal's organ and bassist Eddie Calhoun
78.s: Horace bought Jamal's compact keyboard instrument, used it with the Billy Williams Revue. Bassist Eddie Calhoun, whom Horace taught to read, replaced Crosby and left for Erroll Garner.
78.ch: Portraits from Hemphill to Getz, and the bebop question
78.q: He didn't like it, and it began to be the rage around Chicago, and I -- I tried a little of the Strand where I was playing with my group, that at this Grand Ballroom (Unaudible), and it worked out real good. We -- I had a little keyboard, you know, made, not quite as big as the piano and I pressed…

78.t: John Kirby: tuba, steel string bass and his own sextet
78.s: Kirby, later married to Maxine Sullivan, played tuba with Fletcher, had a six-piece hotel combo and a metal string bass.
78.ch: Portraits from Hemphill to Getz, and the bebop question
78.q: John Kirby. Now there's a guy. He was a real character. You know, John was married to the great singer, Maxine Sullivan. In later years this happened. But John had a great little six piece combo that played some of the major hotels in the country. That was a great group. In fact, that's -- he was a…

256.t: Personnel changes at Friars Inn: Stitzel, Pollack, Steve Brown
256.s: Schoebel and Snyder leave and are replaced by Mel Stitzel, Ben Pollack and Steve Brown, whom he calls the greatest jazz bassist.
256.q: We replaced, uh, Frank Snyder with Ben Pollack, and we replaced Elmer Schoble with Mel Stitzel on piano, then we replaced Arnold Lake Canna with Steve Brown, who to me was the world's greatest jazz bass player. In fact, he started all these guys slapping a bass. No. And I think he's now Secretary…

256.t: Steve Brown's slap bass and other players
256.s: A bassist copies Steve Brown; remarks on trumpeters and New Orleans pianists.
256.q: He was the first guy to slobber around here. We had a guy with Ben Burnie. Ben Burnie was the MC, you know, that's when they're having those stage shows. So this Russian bass player is in the pit, see? So he says, uh, show me how Steve Brown slaps the bass. And I was like, boom, boom, boom, and…

816.t: Basie Mitchell, the bassist who went to California
816.s: They try to identify bassist Basie Mitchell, whose family lived near Warner, and where he is now.
816.q: Uh. I know his family good. They used to live right at the corner from us, Sonny. Yeah. Right at Orleans and Roman. Yeah. Mitchell. Mitchell.

816.t: Old band music, bass parts and artificial notes
816.s: They discuss Red's old music, tough bass parts, and using artificial notes on trombone and valve instruments.
816.ch: Eureka Brass Band and Sonny Henry
816.q: That peg horn in that baritone is missing. Yeah. Because they got some of that, we got some of that old music up there now if Red was to go through it. Show you that old music we used to play. I was showing Sonny a piece there at what you call it? Chicago? Tribune. Chicago Tribune. Chicago Tribune.…

261.t: Favorite bass players: John Porter, John Joseph, Jerry Green, Sidney Brown
261.s: Verrett names the bass players he liked, including Kaiser Joseph, who worked with him at Club Desire.
261.q: John Porter. It's that old man you had last night there. I like to wake him with John Joseph, that's a good man too. I worked with him, I worked with his brother for years. His brother got killed, come to California and got killed. I'm going to be able to kill him.

261.t: Austin Young and the banjoist Gaia at the dance hall
261.s: Russell praises Austin Young; Verrett recalls a band after he left with Gaia, who stayed on one chord.
261.q: Yeah, I know he's a good man. Both of his brothers were good. The sport was real good too. Good musician. Now they worked in the foreign dance after I came out. They worked there for many years.

817.s: He names Bob Haggart and a bass player in a New York band as favorites.
817.q: Yeah. Yeah. Marty Cobb. Bob Haggart. Bob Haggart especially, I think. And there's some colored bass players in New York. One of them with this band, the Paris Brothers. I can't tell you the man's name, but he comes through pretty good on that, too, I think.

817.t: Boyhood bass players: Frank Netto and Pops Foster
817.s: He recalls Frank Netto in a club and identifies Pops Foster with the Armstrong and Luis Russell band, seen at the Coliseum.
817.q: No, I can't remember any of them. No, I can't. There were... Well, wait now. I remember... Seems like I remember Frank Netto. I think I remember Frank playing in the Two Bits Club. Yeah, it cost me.

968.t: Father practicing at home and his bowed bass
968.s: His father practiced at home, was a good chord man who bowed the bass and could be heard from afar.
968.q: Well he always practiced by himself on different things called. He always was a good chord man and a good bull man on bass.

968.t: Soapbox bass demonstration and wrapping up the session
968.s: Russell and others try rubbing a broom, bottle and string to make a homemade bass sound; the talk turns to Dick Allen's tub bass and strings, and the session is closed.
968.q: For more information visit www.fema.org Oh, yeah, and you leave your finger still and just rub the... Yeah, that's too light, huh? Well, will that red share do it? That would do it, huh? Something like that, maybe, but then you can't get on. Wait a minute. So, there's the woo! Okay, just hold your…

972.t: Esau McGee, playing collections and carrying the bass on streetcars
972.s: He played banjo, guitar and bass with Esau McGee around ballrooms for collections, took his bass on electric cars, and recalls it surviving a flood.
972.q: Esau McGee used to play banjo and guitar. What's his name? Esau McGee used to play guitar and banjo. Him and I used to play together. Well I didn't belong to the unit down there. We used to go around, you know, play around in the ballroom, different places, go and pick a collection.

972.s: After the flood he found the bass damaged and recalls the repair, dated to about 1947, before a St. Joseph's night job.
972.q: Yeah, and Lawrence Morello, he had his N-to-five, and his guitar, yeah. Couldn't get down there, take eight days to it. After I go down there, I told my wife, I said, oh baby, what you worried about? I said, oh my, you're seven half-throw instrument. Oh, I went down there, I was sweeping the water.…

675.t: Two-beat bass and the use of the bow
675.s: Russell asks how early bassists played; Braud says two beats and more bow, which modern players neglect.
675.q: Two beats. Two beats. And more of the bow. The bow is very eccentric in some places. Now, the bass players of today, they don't use a bow. They don't know what it's for. See what I mean? And the bass comes in, plays a very big part on the string bass, in places you can use it. You know what I mean?…

675.t: First New Orleans bass players and Steve Brown
675.s: Braud names Kimball and Steve Brown as the first bassists he heard and praises Brown's work with Paul Whiteman and his own care for tone.
675.q: Well, I had them. The first I heard were Billy Murray, Kimball, and Steve Brown, one of the finest, too. I knew him in the front. I'm a Goldcats kitten. Well, he's from New Orleans. Yeah. He played with the Browns Band. He left here with the Browns Band around 1913. And he have a son. I don't know…

284.t: Why the bass is his favourite instrument
284.s: He always listened first to the bass and likes it best.
284.q: I'll tell you, I'll tell you. Player of that, maybe. I don't know why I didn't have a bass long years ago because I always did like the bass.

284.s: A King bass at home and an Epiphone he uses on the job, which is more powerful.
284.q: Yeah, and I'm telling the truth between the two instruments, you know. This one has got a nice sound already now, but the other bass is the Epiphone is more powerful. I had this bass on the job shelf at the time. And I don't know if the people out there could help, but me playing it myself, I can…

638.t: Whereabouts of bassist Chester Zardis, and Slow Drag
638.s: They discuss where Chester Zardis went and praise his bass playing, and Slow Drag's.
638.q: Yeah, he is a good bass player. Yeah, he really is a good bass player. And I tell you, slow drag pretty good bass player from back in his age. Right.

638.t: Slow Drag Pavageau in 1923, Sandpaper George and homemade instruments
638.s: He remembers meeting Slow Drag in 1923, Sandpaper George, and a bass he made out of a box.
638.q: I'm telling you. But they got a lot of young ones now. Get tired. Can't hold up like he do. Can't do like he do. He really works. He works. Now, that's a man started out. I remember slow drag. I remember slow drag in 1923. I met him. A young fella. He came in and another fella he called George.…

766.s: Bama, once a drummer and now a trumpeter, comes from Suburban.
766.q: Oh yeah, he used to play drum, now he plays trumpet now. Yeah, Bama, yeah, that's right, Bama. He's from Seussberry. Seussberry's from Seussberry too. He's from Seussberry. Yeah, big Heverset fella, he used to play drum. Long Salmon.

766.t: Old man Glenny and his three-string bass
766.s: Glenny worked with him for years, began on a three-string bass and used the bow, which Cleo took from him.
766.q: Oh yeah, that's how I worked with that old man Glennie. I mean, he worked with me for years and years. He worked with me for years and years old man Glennie. Every job I had he worked.

128.t: Bud Russo and Little Dad with Punch Miller
128.s: Bud Russo played bass and later in church; Little Dad played banjo with Punch until Punch left for Chicago.
128.q: Yeah, I remember Bud just played bass years ago. Sure stuff But the birth of that was in 44. That's been a long time. I haven't seen the birth for a long while. But last time I see it, Buddy told me he had joined church and he was playing his bass in the church. He told me.

128.t: Little Jim on bass and violin
128.s: Allen and Robinson identify Little Jim, a bass and violin player from the country.
128.q: What else did Jim play? Jim Sussbaum? Mm hmm. Jim's played with, he's a little violin like that. That's his point of his answer. Mm hmm. Violin? Yeah. That's his point of his life, the violin.

140.s: Rowe asks how the bass role changed; Grimes names Pettiford, Ray Brown, Percy Heath.
140.q: It caused more playing than I was doing. It caused more playing to be played by that means. There was bass players like Oscar Pettiford and Ray Brown and Percy Heath and bass players like that, Israel Crosby and two more, you know, very good bass players, technically. I mean you know if you wanted…

140.t: Grimes's encouragers and the bass player's role
140.s: Grimes cites Max Roach and Prez as encouragers; they discuss what the bassist listens to.
140.q: Yes, a lot of professional musicians like Max Roach or the Prez, you know a lot of musicians like that I’ve played with and you know I’d have to go through my struggle up there, which they encouraged me about that.

980.t: Bassists who want to be saxophonists
980.s: Rowe and Caine agree some bassists show off; the bass job is like the offensive line.
980.q: Yeah. Kind of like the offensive line in football you know. Like kind of do the job.

980.t: Playing other people's basses with pickups
980.s: Using borrowed amplified basses changes his approach; he wants a pretty but nasty sound with no frills.
980.q: Well I just deal with — I deal with whatever. I mean I have, I’ll say this, now that happens. And if it’s a bass that’s set up for only an amp, like I’ll try to use it acoustically. But some basses you get and the action is this high, and you literally — so there’s been probably five to ten times…

420.t: Acoustic bass versus pickups and the stick bass
420.s: He argues an acoustic bass should sound acoustic, and discusses the stick bass and Bob Cranshaw's travel bass.
420.q: Yeah, okay. Well I can go off from there, because if it’s an acoustic bass, it should be acoustic. Bing. The thing was made with this big piece of wood for a reason. That’s so the wood moves the air, not so that it moves some little Piezo electric invaders that were stuck into the bridge to induce…

420.t: Bass players he went to hear: Slam Stewart and others
420.s: He recalls Slam Stewart with Illinois Jacquet, Milt Hinton, Duvivier and Mraz.
420.q: To go see? Slam Stewart. One of my favorite nights of jazz I ever heard was Slam with Illinois Jacquet. It was a quartet setting at the Village Vanguard. And he didn’t use any amp and he had gut strings on an old Kay bass with a little ribbon microphone out front. Sounded great. That was one of my…

580.t: Following Scott LaFaro and the new bass approach
580.s: Israels says LaFaro wasn't alone in the new bass approach; Haden, Stinson, Swallow and he were also hearing more than quarter notes, with Pettiford an influence.
580.q: No. There was, as often happens in the world it’s rarely one person who comes up with whatever it is that the new thing is. It does happen occasionally. I just heard an interesting podcast about a Hungarian woman scientist who was the instigator of the MRNA technology that — the biological…

580.t: Humphrey Lyttelton's tribute and Israels' melodic bass style
580.s: Rowe reads Lyttelton's 1965 praise; Israels downplays virtuosity, stressing melodic playing, with Pettiford and Red Mitchell as models.
580.q: Well he gives me too much credit for virtuosity. Well too much — it’s how he saw it. It was his perception of it. And maybe the perception of some other people. From my perspective, knowing my limitations in terms of virtuosity and technical prowess I think I used my abilities efficiently and…

135.t: Ray Brown's 'spider' fingering and Oscar Pettiford
135.s: Heath explains what Ray Brown showed him about hand position, why Oscar Pettiford was his idol, and that Pettiford wrote 'One Bass Hit'.
135.ch: Founding the MJQ and bass craft
135.q: Ray Brown showed me how, when I just bought the bass, there was a certain way of grabbing the neck, it can’t be spoken how, but grabbing the neck like… Oscar Pettiford never stood up on the thumb and played like that, Oscar Pettiford had perfect pitch. And you asked me about my idols, that was my…

135.t: Buying the Rogeri bass in Berlin, 1956
135.s: Heath tells how Michelot found an old Rogeri-style bass, how he borrowed $1,000 from the Quartet, and its later restoration by Barry Kolstein.
135.q: maker of mine. I had some papers from Frederick Bohm that said at the time in ’56 that my bass was over 250 years old in a Rogeri style from Cremona. I don’t know what I did with the papers. I left them in a cab somewhere in Italy ‘cause I was never gonna sell that bass. I didn’t need no papers…

226.t: Bass role models: Pettiford, Slam Stewart, Jimmy Blanton
226.s: He names Oscar Pettiford, Slam Stewart and Blanton, who revolutionized the bass in the Ellington band.
226.ch: Depression-era Chicago: jobs, marriage, first bands
226.q: Also would be Oscar Pettiford and people like that that I knew of – great bass players. Slam Stewart. [I] knew about them. And of course, later on, [Jimmy] Blanton with the Duke Ellington band. He was the youngest of all of them. I didn’t ever know him or get to – I only heard him play in person…

226.t: Buying the white plywood bass at Wurlitzer
226.s: He picked a cheaper white bass that sounded great, kept it his whole career and finally gave it away.
226.q: I went down to get a bass. I was going to try out just – I knew I needed a bass, so I went to, here again, Wurlitzer, which is downtown. They have new pianos and new basses. They had basses all in a rack – on a rack, about maybe 12 or 13 string basses. I went along and tried each one of them and…

400.t: Walter Wright, a bassist idol who aged out of the work
400.s: Hinton describes Walter Wright, who refused a New Year's Eve gig after no calls all year.
400.ch: Cotton Club, Zutty and Chicago traditions
400.q: Yeah. Walter Wright, very wonderful bassist, a New Orleans… tall, dignified, a no frills guy. Sometimes the no frills guy didn‟t get through because he didn‟t take a partying and all that kind of stuff.

400.t: Carl Pruitt and Jimmy Blanton, who revolutionized bass
400.s: Hinton says Blanton destroyed the earlier bassists and recalls the Downbeat criticism of Duke Ellington's bass duets.
400.ch: Studio years, bass choir and bass philosophy
400.q: He destroyed all of us but he came out and we got [unintelligible] threatened to burn up my bass but he came from violinist standpoint like me but he developed it a thousand times more then I had with his wonderful long fingers that he had. To speak of that, when he first came on, Avan Anderson…

379.t: Finding bass players who can play Cuban style
379.s: American bassists struggle; he praises a few players and Jorge Dalto.
379.q: Yeah. I had a few guys, that if you had take (inaudible), all you had to do, write two bars (inaudible). The straight basses, no.

379.t: Cuban bass foundation in rock and roll
379.s: He heard Quincy Jones's TV theme and calls Cuba the foundation of American bass patterns.
379.q: But I don't know the title of the program, what it was. And it was amazing, when I heard this bass starting in, how he developed the thing, and then got into the theme. And a couple of days after, Chico __________ said, you know, we've been sleeping, we've been discriminated our own self and our…

90.t: Tweed Beard and the Glenn Miller era
90.s: Working with bassist Tweed Beard around the time Glenn Miller was hot.
90.q: Let's see. I started working with a bass player out of Columbus, Ohio, named Tweed(?) Beard around this time. And he was... He wasn't the greatest bass player, but he could make a great presentation, you know, and he was a pretty boy and everything. And he always had good guys around him. That's…

90.t: Pianist Duke Brooks and bassist Iggy Shavack
90.s: Remembering pianist Duke Brooks and bassist Iggy Shavack.
90.ch: Howard McGhee's band and bebop in LA
90.q: I'd like to mention a piano player who was a terrific guy and a fantastic piano player. His name was Duke Brooks. And he recorded with me later. I'll get into that later, but I wanted to make sure I mentioned his name. He was killed hoboing back to Kansas City to see his mother, on the train, and…

170.t: The bass Oscar Pettiford gave him
170.s: Art Blakey tries to buy him a bass but Pettiford offers him an old German flatback, and the fiddle is often pawned.
170.ch: Riverside and the New York scene
170.q: Sure. He took me down and said, 'pick you out one' -- I didn't want him to buy this fiddle that he picked out, because I wanted a fiddle that was already broken in, you might say -- you know, I thought, tell him, let's go to a pawn shop, but he didn't have that kind of cash money to put out in…

170.t: Young bassists, Stanley Clarke and Paul Jeffrey's 1972 date
170.s: Ware marvels at Stanley Clarke reading Paul Jeffrey's charts but misses their bottom.
170.ch: Bass playing, avant-garde and the state of the music
170.q: Well, that's true, but most of them think, "Oh, I know music backwards and forward," you know, that they qualify to play anything. But that's not the way it is really. To play just straight-ahead music. Anybody can write anything for you. They write solos for guys and they can play them. I marvel…

75.s: Organ bass lacks definition, so players fill in; conflicts with a bass player's line.
75.ch: Eddie Heywood, the organ and later work
75.q: Only certain organs have that bass tone, the dominant bass tone. If you were using that in conjunction

75.s: He explains foot manuals, the hand bass extension and heel-and-toe, and Virgil Fox.
75.ch: Eddie Heywood, the organ and later work
75.q: : Well, actually... You can play that. But then there's another extension on the hand manual of the bass. So actually you're not playing with your foot all the time. You're playing the bass with your hand. But it gives it the illusion you're playing with your feet.

171.t: Double-jointed fingers and high strings on the bass
